Q1 Answer

The textbook idea is that if a company gains near 100% market share, they can set prices much higher, than if there were many competitors. A Monopolist is big enough that they can simply buy the competition or in an area with an emerging competitor, the monopolist can afford maintaining their market share, by setting prices so low they will take losses for a while, until the competitor goes out of business.

Classic examples of a monopoly are De Beers Diamonds and Rockefeller + Standard Oil. Even those cases are debatable though...

Q2 Answer

Laissez faire (French for "let do") doesn't mean "no taxation", just relatively little and very loose regulations. Take for example Child labor, 12 hour work days and pollution in the early days of the Industrial Revolution. Basically Laissez faire prefers economic output over negative externalities that may occur as a result. You seem to make the assumption that places with higher taxes and regulations are automatically bad. If regulations are effective, they can reduce negative externalities. Additionally, if there is low corruption and social benefits from tax money could are spread out reasonably, it could benefit everyone. For example everyone can enjoy the benefits of clean air and water, as well as an educated population with high employment that commits less crimes. If everyone has food, water and shelter, there is less incentive for social unrest.

Those who support laissez-faire capitalist generally tend to argue that any disruption in the natural state of things will be corrected by future competition or consumer response. So if somebody creates a coercive monopoly then there is room for a new competitor to come in to offer lower prices and reshape the market.

This doesn't really work out in reality. The thing that that ideology ignores is barriers to entry and expected competition. So there is actually a good example in the telecoms market in the US. The reason many people think Comcast/Time Warner have a monopoly is because of government protectionism. To a degree this is certainly true. They have exclusive service contracts in some areas and they can also do things like prevent other companies from utilizing their infrastructure (like utility poles) in setting up their own infrastructure. However, the real problem is much deeper than just government.

Google managed to overcome the governmental barriers to entry and the economic barriers to entry with Google Fiber and still was a complete failure. Why is this? It comes back to expected competition. Google announces they're coming to an area and will offer service to compete with the local Comcast monopoly. Every rejoices and pledges to sign up by the millions. Google spends billions of dollars and years of time laying down their infrastructure, setting up their local offices, and so on. 24 hours before they finally 'flip the switch' and allow for signups Comcast, "Oh yeah. We're going to price and service match everything Google is offering." And nobody swaps over. Google Fiber has been operational for 5 years now in areas with millions of potential subscribers. They ended up with an estimated 450,000 cable subscribers and 70,000 television subscribers. They've recently announced they're scaling back operations which is signaling their intentions to pull out of this disaster.

You can't just compete against the coercive monopoly's prices, but you have to be able to compete against them price matching you. In the end in a true and completely competitive free market companies would kill themselves. Prices would go so low that the smallest disruption in expectation would bankrupt companies. And the people running companies aren't stupid. This is why collusion naturally emerges. And with the collusion comes orchestrated offers to prevent competition. You don't even need government for this. Imagine you have a monopoly on wooden chairs. You sell them at a huge markup and so somebody decides to try to come compete. You don't need to get the government to stop him, simply let the lumber mill in on your inflate profits. So long as the lumber mill is driven just by profit, which is supposed to be the driving force of capitalism, it would be in their interest to only service you.

Regulation is completely mandatory for a functional economy because of this natural tendency towards collusion and anti competitiveness in capitalism. The problem of course is regulatory capture. For instance in the US the head of food regulation was a Monsanto VP/lawyer. So we got things like farmers being eligible for a substantially subsidized insurance discount from the government but only if they swapped over to GMO seed - which Monsanto had an effective monopoly on. It's a complete bastardization of the market because of regulatory capture. Scandinavia is so successful not only because they have strong regulations but because they have, so far, managed to keep corruption to a minimum. That is the tricky part the key to success. There's a lot of correlations that can give us a hint, but they also end up begging the question of are they causing less corruption or is less corruption caused by them? For instance wealth inequality and corruption have a very strong link but which causes which? Or perhaps neither of them are the independent variable and there's some other factor, perhaps cultural, that strengths both. In the US there's a bit of a culture of wealth worship. Cultures like this would tend to drive wealth inequality and corruption independently. Tough questions that there's no accepted answer to.
